speechtext: Because your government closed it down in 1930.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext:
The minister can make a cheap gibe at me, but I am not going to reply in kind. Our government had to meet circumstances as they arose in a very trying time, and times that were not of our making. Whether we were right or wrong does not alter the situation. The fact of the matter is that Canadian Airways was an attempt on the part of private enterprise to enter a new field of transportation in this country, and it did not survive. I do not suggest for a moment that the minister believes that governmental action was the 'cause of its death. At all events When the ifnihister entered this federal area in 1938 he himself encouraged the policy of private enterprise, but because of the amount of the capital required, because of the size of the country, because of the magnitude of the undertaking then under review, it was felt

Aeronautics Act
that only strong and important bodies could go into this business of transcontinental airways.
But private enterprise was encouraged; that was the policy of the government, and I think I can say without fear of successful contradiction that from that day down to a comparatively recent time the administration opposite encouraged private enterprise to go into the field of aviation. Had it not been for the nature of the huge undertaking, much more would have been done than was done by private enterprise. In any event I think it is incontrovertible that when the small lines reached the end of their tether because they could not make any money and could not pay their way, the government of the day, which was the present government, unquestionably encouraged the taking over of those lines by Canadian Pacific Air Lines. I do not think there is any doubt about that. They invested a large sum of money in those lines, which I believe is now in danger. However, I have had no communication with Canadian Pacific Air Lines, and I am not dealing with that aspect at all to-day.
In 1938, then, we had a policy set up of quasi-private enterprise, shall I say, of course aided by governmental subventions without which it never could have been started. There were substantial and generous subventions from the Post Office Department, and I am not sure that the minister is wrong when he suggests that in a given case these subventions should take another form. I am inclined to agree with that part of the bill which suggests that if public aid is required it should not be in the form of swollen post office subventions, because I believe the revenues of the Post Office Department are being unduly loaded with expenditures that are not justified from an operating, departmental view. However, I have no doubt there are two schools of thought in that regard. I have not investigated the matter mathematically, and I am not sure which school is right, but I am not condemning the minister's point of view in that Tegard.
Then suddenly, after the Canadian people and particularly the youth of Canada had become air-minded,'we had a right-about-face on the part of the administration, and this bill is the result. I venture to say to this committee and to the country that we have never been given, at any time or at any place, a satisfactory reason for the change in policy. The government sold its policy on this matter to the house and the country in 1938; now it has changed its policy, and it must justify that change in policy at the bar of public opinion. If it was right then it is wrong now;
if it is right now it was wrong six years ago. Not once, as far as I can recall, has the minister justified his right-about-face in regard to this question of public policy.
On the question of public policy I assert, as was asserted by my colleague a few minutes ago, that on questions of policy the government of the day must, of course, have the last word; but because the government asserts a policy does not by any means carry with it the conviction that such policy is right. No board of aeronautics; no governmental judicial body such as has been set up in relation to railways, has the right to determine public policy. That is the function of the executive, supported by parliament; but once that function has been discharged the duty of the executive should cease, and the operation of carrying out the policy should be vested in a judicial body which would be free from political control. That, I believe, has been the history of the railway commission and should be the pattern for dealing with aeronautics in this country. What have we here? We have an emasculated board of aeronautics which is to be set up under this bill, which has nothing whatever to do with policy but which is purely advisory, and that is the most you can say for it. It is true that in the bill the minister has gone through the form of giving this body certain authority. Section 8 provides that it may make rules for the regulation of its proceedings and the performance of its functions and duties under this measure. That means it can draw up a set of by-laws, and that is all it means; it may make rules for the orderly carrying out of the business within its jurisdiction. Then section 9 provides:
Subject to the directions of the minister, the board shall from time to time make investigations and surveys relating to the operation and development of commercial air services in Canada. . . .
This board has no independent function delegated to it by parliament. It is a puppet of the minister, and I use that word in no derogatory sense; it is a term very commonly used to designate people in the category in which the membership of this board will find themselves, in that they cannot move without the nod and the authority, express or implied, of the minister. It does not take a board to make explorations, investigations and surveys. Competent departmental officials can perform these functions. The minister might as well have gone the whole way and reserved the whole power to the department in question. The board is given a power not with respect to policy but with respect to making recommendations in reference to any investigation or sur-
Aeronautics Act

vey it may make, and to advise the minister in the exercise of his duties and powers under this measure in all matters relating to civil aviation. Under that provision I suppose they are to be, in a sense, a board of experts who tender their advice, which may or may not be accepted. Nothing could be much more innocuous than a board of this nature, set up to do the bidding and will of the minister if they will, but if they do not conform to his desires then their reports go into the waste-paper basket unless he chooses to adopt them. Of course that is no kind of judicial board at all. It is not an administrative board. That is merely an advisory committee that could be set up without any legislation. As far as sections 8 and 9 of the bill are concerned, I believe "innocuous" is the right term for them. There is a further question in section 10:
The iboard shall from time to time make recommendations to the minister with reference to any investigation or survey made by it. . . .
And so on. That is in the same category as section 9. Then section 11 empowers the board, subject to the approval of the governor in council, to make certain regulations. In this case the governor in council is the minister, because this board will report to the minister, and if he does not see fit to recommend these regulations to the governor in council for enactment they die then and there. Any report the minister may make to the governor in council either pro or con, favourable or unfavourable, will, of course, be given either the approval or the disapproval of the governor in council. The minister still remains the head, the neck, the shoulders and everything else, so far as the board is concerned.
Someone has said that he will be a dictator. The minister's reply to that is that somebody has to be a dictator. I do not think anyone has to be a dictator in respect of a great utility, such as aviation in this country. Let us put it on a plane analogous to the manner in which our railways are controlled in Canada, md that will be suitable to the people. The oeople of Canada will never again allow the control and operation of ralways in their country to fall back into the hands of a min-.ster of railways, or a minister of transport, whatever you wish to call him, as existed prior to 1904.
Here is a government inviting parliament, commanding its followers, to put aviation in exactly the position the people of Canada would reject in connection with railway transportation. I submit that in respect of the principle involved the two cases are analogous. If it is a proper principle that the railways shall be controlled in the manner I have indicated-perhaps inadequately-then it is

just as true that the control of aeronautics and the operation of companies, or whoever
may be fortunate enough to get licences, should be carried on in the same way as is done by the board of transport commissioners. I believe that when the people of Canada come to understand the tremendous powers vested in the minister designated-the Minister of Munitions and Supply-they will reject this bill, because they will know that it is capable of the greatest possible abuse.
The minister says that he will operate fairly, and I have no doubt that is his present intention. But let me put this case to him: In the face of an election one group of citizens comes to him with a proposal, and another group approaches him with another proposal in respect of the same subject matter. He must make the decision. What minister ought to allow himself to be placed in that position? I say that no minister ought to permit himself to be so placed.
Let me illustrate by referring to the granting of pensions by the Minister of Pensions and National Health. It is unthinkable that the Minister of Pensions and National Health should be authorized by parliament to grant pensions in individual cases. It is equally unthinkable that the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the minister designated by this bill, should be allowed to choose as between groups A, B, C and D as to which shall have a licence to operate an air route.
The Canadian people do not like this power of picking and choosing at the whim or, if you like, the prejudice of a minister. Or, yes, it may be the caprice of a minister. I point this out as a principle which ought to guide parliament in dealing with this matter. A minister ought not to allow himself to be put in a position where he will have to decide as between different applicants for licences. It is not fair to the minister, and by every test it is not fair to the people that the minister should have this power.
One board has issued licences to aviation corporations in this country. This new board is to have the power to override the decision of the present board, which is a branch of the board of transport commissioners. It can override a licence already given. The new board will have power to review all licences with respect to commercial air services issued under part III of the Transport Act, 1938, or under part VII of the air regulations of the same year, legislation set up under this very minister. What an incongruous position! Is parliament going to set up a new board to review the actions of a board which previously, by the will of parliament, was granted control over the issuing of certain licences? I think

Aeronautics Act
that is a terrible position. Here we have a right. of appeal, an overriding veto on a creature of a judicial or corporate nature the minister has already set up. Or, to be more exact, there is to be an overriding veto in a given case, if it is so issued, from the decision of a judicial board in which the minister himself, through parliament, vested full authority in connection with these licences.
I would ask the minister, when he replies, to give me an answer to that. Why is there a violation of a principle whereby one board of equal standing is to have power to review the activities of another board of similar standing, and probably without the hearing of any evidence at all? If there were a higher judicial authority, my argument would not prevail. But I have only to mention the lack of principle underlying the power given to this new board, without any reason, to review licences which have been issued.
Then, of course, there is the question of the licences themselves, a subject which has been debated to some extent. The board is not to issue licences. I know the bill says that the board may issue to any person a licence, but that provision is subject to an overriding stipulation that the minister must give his approval first. That does not leave the board to act as a free agent. Every consideration of public policy, public convenience and public demand, in the interests of right, justice and equity, might prompt a board to come to the conclusion that a licence should be issued. Yet that licence would be refused if the minister said "No", and there is no appeal from his decision.
There is a form of appeal-I venture to say it is just a hollow mockery-from the decision of the board. The only other mockery in government legislation which would be comparable is found in tire taxation laws of the dominion. I have run up against them lately-not on my own behalf, but for somebody else. I find that if a taxpayer in this country is dissatisfied with his assessment under the income tax or excess profits tax laws, he may file a notice of appeal. To whom does he appeal? He appeals to the very authority which imposed the tax in the first instance, namely the Minister of National Revenue. It is a travesty in the administration of justice that such should be the case, and I have urged upon certain persons in governmental authority that an amendment should be made at this parliament. Appeals from assessments under the income tax and excess profits tax laws should not be from Caesar to Caesar, from minister to minister, or from the minister who made the decision and the assessment to the minister who is acting in the capacity of an appellate court.

I am satisfied that the conviction will be brought into the mind of every one who is listening that the system is all wrong. There should be an appeal to a judicial body and it should be an appeal on the question both of law and of fact. In principle it will be an appeal on the question of the interpretation of the statute. I suppose that here again the bureaucratic mind which is so much in evidence today is again prevailing. There is to be an appeal from a body dominated by the minister to the minister who dominated the body in the first instance. I do not think I could use more cogent language to condemn that provision of the statute if I were to stand here all night. I condemn the underlying principle of this bill. If hon. members will do themselves, not me, and the country the justice that they ought to do by reading and studying these provisions, I do not think one of them will vote for this section. I condemn the provisions that maintain the incongruity of keeping in the hands of the minister absolute, unthrottled, uncontrolled control of the operations of this board.
It is a farce to set up a board of this nature. A board of aeronautic engineers, under salary, under the minister's direction, could do all the work that this board is intended to do. I suppose it is being set up under the guise that it is an independent board, but it is nothing of the sort. From A to Z this will be a creature of the minister and nothing else. I had not intended to speak so long, but if [DOT] an amendment is moved to subsection 1 of section 12 to strike out the words "subject to the approval of the minister," I intend to vote in favour of it and endeavour to give this board some independence. Subsection 2 of that section provides:
No such licence shall be issued in respect of a commercial air service, owned, leased, controlled or operated by any person who is engaged in the transport of goods-
I am not just sure of the implication of that, but I desire to call the attention of the committee to the. overriding provision which follows:
-unless the governor in council is of opinion that it is in the public interest _ that such licence be issued.
Let us consider the implication of that.

subtopic: CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES- AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
speechtext: I do not like to see this bill pass without voicing my objections to some of its provisions. The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) referred to the fact that before a railway could be established the promoters had to come to this parliament to obtain an act. Under the present Transport Act, part III, I believe it is provided that before the existing transport board can grant licences to companies or persons to carry on aviation the governor in council shall state between what places in this country lines may be run or carried on. But once that is done, the transport board has absolute jurisdiction.

I understood that the hon. member was making a wide distinction between the powers of railway companies and those of aviation companies or persons carrying on aviation. When this committee was last sitting on Monday evening, the minister said, as reported at page 3969 of Hansard, that the bill proposed to set up a board that had all the judicial or quasi-judicial functions of the board of transport commissioners, under the Transport Act, and that those functions were not subject to review by the minister. He went on to say that provision was made in the bill for an appeal to the minister in certain cases, just as there is provision for an appeal from the board of transport commissioners to the privy council.
If you will examine the transport commission's powers, which are contained in section 13 of the Transport Act, you will find that the commission was empowered to license aircraft to transport passengers or goods. They were given absolute power. The power was not limited. They did not have to obtain the approval of the minister before granting those licences. It was, I say, an absolute power. But when you come to examine this bill, you find that the powers of the board are limited. Its powers are restricted by section 12, subsection 1, which provides that it may issue licences only with the approval of the minister. The board is limited further in its powers to grant licences by section 12, subsection 4, of the bill, which provides that it cannot issue a licence until the minister issues an operating

certificate; to save time I will refrain from reading subsection 4, but in substance that is the provision it makes.
Many hon. members on this side have asked why the board's powers have been so limited, and I have not heard a satisfactory reply from the minister. As the hon. member for Lake Centre said the other evening, there are no safeguards in the bill against objectionable exercise or abuse of the minister's powers.
I do not mean by that, and I do not think he did, that the present minister would indulge in or exercise any powers that might be called abuses. Nevertheless, in my opinion, and as the hon. member for Vancouver South said, the bill confers dictatorial powers on the minister and that, I think, is objectionable.
But the conferring of these powers on the minister is not all that is objectionable in the bill. The bill provides for an appeal by an applicant who feels that he has not received a fair deal. But to whom is he to appeal? Who is to hear and decide on his grievance? The Minister of Transport, the man who has the say as to whether or not he gets the licence, is the man who is to judge whether or not his appeal will be allowed.
There is no principle of justice in such a proceeding, no principle on which such a proceeding can be justified. Under our system of democratic government, the men and women the voters of the country elect to parliament make the laws, and independent judges interpret and enforce those laws. We have been inclined at times to be rather slack in our duty in the making of these laws. We have been inclined at times, instead of making laws, to allow laws to be made by means of regulations. If such regulations are merely of an administrative nature, there is no great objection; but when laws are made by regulations which impose penalties, then there is great objection.
The laws of the dominion should be made in this chamber, with the suggestions and criticisms of members of parliament. We should not allow legislative boards or civil servants to carry out the duties we were elected to discharge, and members of parliament are negligent in their duty to their constituents as well as in their duty to the country if they permit the laws of the dominion to be made by regulations, the berms of which they do not know and which they have not passed on or approved.
But, sir, that is not the only objection to this bill. It is not only the matter of regulations that I object to, but the powers that are conferred on the minister, who can act as a court

of appeal and decide upon, grievances when he is in the first place the one who has already come to a decision as to whether or not a licence shall be granted.
